title: On the Transfiguration of the Lord
subtitle: A homily on Tabor and the unveiled glory of the divinity
source: A retelling in our words of the homily on the Transfiguration handed down under St. Ephraim's name. No public-domain English translation of it has been found, so these are not his words. By the editors of Purify.

sections.title: Why He led them up the mountain
paragraphs: The homily begins with the reason for the ascent. The Lord led the three disciples up the mountain to show them His kingship before His passion and His glory before His dishonour, so that when they saw Him taken and crucified they would know that He suffered not from weakness but of His own will, for the salvation of the world.

He showed them the glory of His divinity before the Resurrection too, so that when He rose they would know that the glory was not a reward newly given for His labour, but His own before the ages with the Father, the glory He spoke of as He went to His passion (John 17:5).
notes: The homily's pastoral logic is simple: the Apostles will see the Cross, and before they see the Cross they need to have seen the Glory.

sections.title: Two suns on the mountain
paragraphs: On the mountain the disciples saw the glory of the divinity that His humanity had hidden: His face shining like lightning and His garments white as light, as if there were two suns, the one in the sky and the one in His face, which only they were given to see.

sections.title: The light flooded from Him
paragraphs: The whiteness of His garments showed that the light came from within, from the divinity, shining through His whole body: not a brightness laid on Him from outside, as on the face of Moses (Exodus 34:29-35), but His own.
Nor did that light come from elsewhere, or leave Him; and He showed them not the whole depth of His glory, only as much as their eyes could bear.
notes: The contrast with Moses is the turn of the homily. Moses came down from Sinai with a brightness on his face reflected from the glory he had stood near; on Tabor the brightness came from within Christ, because the glory was His own.
